title: Reconstruction of the superstatistical temperature distribution from single-particle kinetic energies
abstract: The framework of superstatistics can be used to describe non-Maxwellian single-particle velocity distributions as mixtures of Maxwellian distributions, where the weight is imposed by a probability density associated to the inverse temperature $β= 1/(k_B T)$. Among the typical model choices for $β$ are gamma, inverse gamma and lognormal distributions, sometimes called the universality classes of superstatistics. Given a set of observed velocities, however, there is no direct method to determine the underlying temperature distribution, as temperature itself is not a phase-space observable, and numerically inverting the Laplace transform is an unreliable process. In this work, we show that Jaynes' principle of maximum entropy can be used to successfully reconstruct the inverse temperature distribution from data, by using the logarithmic moments of the kinetic energy as constraints. Although the kinetic energy distributions for the three universality classes are almost indistinguishable at the same mean and variance of $β$, the method correctly discriminates between them.
summary: This paper develops a method to reconstruct the underlying superstatistical temperature distribution from measured single-particle kinetic energies. By employing Jaynes' maximum entropy principle constrained by logarithmic moments, the authors successfully distinguish between three theoretical universality classes (Gamma, Inverse Gamma, Lognormal). This work provides a robust theoretical tool for analyzing non-Maxwellian statistical systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing the underlying superstatistical inverse temperature distribution ($ eta$) from observed single-particle kinetic energy data.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrate that using Jaynes' maximum entropy principle, constrained by the logarithmic moments of the kinetic energy, can accurately reconstruct the distribution for three distinct superstatistical universality classes.
method: The core method involves applying the maximum entropy principle, maximizing relative entropy subject to constraints derived from the logarithmic moments of the kinetic energy distribution.
model_or_system: The study uses the framework of superstatistics, which models non-Maxwellian velocity distributions as mixtures of Maxwellian distributions weighted by a probability density for the inverse temperature $ eta$. Three specific universality classes—Gamma, Inverse Gamma, and Lognormal—are analyzed.
key_observables: Single-particle kinetic energy distribution $P(k|\lambda)$, the superstatistical inverse temperature distribution $P( eta|\lambda)$, and the dimensionless relative inverse temperature variance $u$.
important_parameters: The mean inverse temperature ($ eta_S$) and the dimensionless relative variance ($u$) are key parameters used to characterize the distributions.
main_assumptions: The reconstruction relies on the assumption that the underlying distribution can be accurately determined by constraining the maximum entropy functional using the logarithmic moments of the kinetic energy.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the reconstructed inverse temperature and kinetic energy distributions for the three classes. Figure 2 compares the three classes' kinetic energy distributions, showing their near indistinguishability. Figure 3 presents the worst-case signed relative errors for estimating $u$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the superstatistical framework and the difficulty of direct inversion. It then details the maximum entropy approach using logarithmic moment constraints. Finally, it presents the results, demonstrating the successful reconstruction and discrimination between the three universality classes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous application of maximum entropy methods to infer underlying physical parameters from complex, non-equilibrium distributions is a powerful theoretical tool applicable to analyzing complex quantum measurements or system dynamics.
